---
title: "Contours traced in the engine"
description: "mark_contour() and mark_contour_filled() trace iso-lines with vellum's own marching squares, so contour lines are chained polylines and filled bands are closed rings — no extra package involved."
categories: [Statistical, Heatmaps]
image: figs/contours-filled.png
---



A contour plot needs somebody to walk a grid of values and chain the crossings
into curves. vellum does that itself (`vellum::vl_contour()`, marching squares),
so `mark_contour()` needs no tracing package: each contour comes back as one
chained polyline, with closed loops actually closed, rather than a heap of
disconnected line segments that happen to line up.

The classic two-cluster density: Old Faithful's eruption lengths against the
wait before them.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
p <- vplot(faithful, width = 7, height = 4.6) |>
  mark_point(x = eruptions, y = waiting, size = 1.6, color = "#3a2f1e", alpha = 0.5) |>
  mark_contour(x = eruptions, y = waiting, bins = 9, linewidth = 0.7) |>
  labs(
    title = "Old Faithful, contoured",
    x = "eruption length (min)", y = "wait before it (min)", color = "density"
  )
```
:::



::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](figs/contours-lines.png){width=100%}
:::
:::


Levels are coloured for you: `mark_contour()` maps `color = after_stat(level)`,
so the legend reads as density without you asking for it.

## Filled bands

`mark_contour_filled()` paints the bands between the levels instead. Each band is
a closed ring, painted in level order, which is what produces the layered look —
and because the rings are real paths rather than a rasterised heatmap, they stay
crisp in SVG and PDF.

A band whose contour runs off the edge of the estimation grid is closed along the
grid boundary rather than chorded shut, so the outermost level fills the corners
it should instead of slicing wedges across the panel.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
p2 <- vplot(faithful, width = 7, height = 4.6) |>
  mark_contour_filled(x = eruptions, y = waiting, bins = 9) |>
  labs(
    title = "The same density, filled",
    x = "eruption length (min)", y = "wait before it (min)", fill = "level"
  )
```
:::



::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](figs/contours-filled.png){width=100%}
:::
:::


## Any surface, not only a density

By default the field is a kernel density estimate of the `x`/`y` cloud (the one
part that still needs `MASS`). Map a `z` aesthetic instead and the mark contours
*your* surface over a regular grid — a fitted response, a simulated field, anything
you can write as a function of two variables.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
grid <- expand.grid(x = seq(-3, 3, length.out = 80), y = seq(-3, 3, length.out = 80))
grid$z <- with(grid, sin(x * 1.4) * cos(y * 1.4) + 0.25 * (x - y))

p3 <- vplot(grid, width = 7, height = 4.6) |>
  mark_contour(x = x, y = y, z = z, bins = 14, linewidth = 0.6) |>
  labs(title = "A supplied surface, not a density", x = NULL, y = NULL, color = "z")
```
:::



::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](figs/contours-surface.png){width=100%}
:::
:::


Note the grid convention: like `image()`, `contour()`, and `outer()`, rows index
`x` and columns index `y`. Pair the lines with
[`mark_text_path()`](text-path.qmd) to label a level directly on its own curve
instead of through a legend.
